---
title: "Introduction to Ethical Issues"
---

## Overview

As explored on the home page, the rise of AI in hiring raises serious ethical questions
about fairness, trust, and transparency. This page takes a closer look at each of those
concerns and what they mean for both job applicants and employers.

---

## Fairness

Fairness is one of the most immediate concerns. Applicants who use AI tools to tailor
their resumes may have a significant advantage over those who do not, whether due to
lack of access, lack of awareness, or a personal choice not to use AI. This creates an
uneven playing field before anyone even reaches an interview.

Some applicants use AI as a shortcut to adjust a base resume for each job posting.
Others go further by adding keywords specifically chosen to pass automated screening
systems. In both cases, the resume may no longer reflect the applicant's genuine
qualifications. Research shows this trend is growing, as seen in the
[AI in Resume Review](https://research-ebsco-com.content.elibrarymn.org/c/nfiawx/search/details/r7coeehicj?db=f6h&limiters=None&q=resume%20AND%20%22artificial%20intelligence%22&searchMode=boolean)
study and this [NYT report](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/07/business/ai-chatbot-prompts-resumes.html).

---

## Transparency

Transparency matters because employers often have no way of knowing how much of a
resume was written by AI. A hiring manager reading a polished, well-structured resume
may assume it reflects the applicant's own communication skills, when in reality it
was heavily rewritten by a language model.

Some companies have begun experimenting with AI-detection tools, but these are
unreliable and raise their own fairness concerns, particularly for non-native English
speakers whose writing may be flagged incorrectly. The
[ProQuest ethics article](https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/ai-ethics-david-goliath-value-conflicts-between/docview/3035302150/se-2?accountid=351)
explores this tension in depth.

---

## Bias

AI tools are not neutral. They are trained on existing data, which means they can
reproduce and amplify existing biases in hiring. Research has shown that name-based
discrimination remains a problem, and AI screening systems have been found to
perpetuate this — see the
[name discrimination study](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/395262744_The_Name_Game_Algorithmic_Gatekeeping_and_the_Systematic_Exclusion_of_Ethnic_Names_in_Digital_Hiring)
for specific findings.

---

## Accessibility

Not everyone has equal access to AI tools. Premium AI writing assistants often require
paid subscriptions, meaning applicants from lower-income backgrounds may not have
access to the same tools as other candidates. This could widen existing inequalities
in the job market rather than reducing them.

---

## Creativity & Trust

When employers suspect resumes are AI-generated, it erodes trust in the hiring process
overall. At the same time, there are concerns that AI-assisted writing reduces an
applicant's creative self-expression and ability to communicate in their own voice —
a concern examined directly in the
[AI & creativity research](https://research-ebsco-com.content.elibrarymn.org/c/nfiawx/search/details/4n2bgsiiqb?db=f6h&limiters=None&q=resume%20AND%20%22artificial%20intelligence%22%20AND%20creativity&searchMode=boolean).

---

## Discussion Questions

1. Is the connection between culture and applicants' stories seen in applications? How has it changed?
2. Should employers treat AI-assisted resumes differently from fully human-written resumes? Why or why not?
3. Does access to AI technology create an unfair advantage for some applicants?
4. How can companies verify that the skills listed on resumes are genuine?
5. Should there be limits on how much AI can be used in the hiring process?

---
